items.title: nvidia/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017-NVFP4
items.content:
# Model Overview ## Description: The NVIDIA DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 NVFP4 model is the quantized version of DeepSeek AI's DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 model, which is an auto-regressive language model that uses an optimized transformer architecture. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 is a natively multimodal Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model with a Causal Encoder-Decoder (CED) architecture, Compressed Sparse Attention 2 (CSA2), and support for contexts of up to one million tokens. For more information, please check [here](https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017). The NVIDIA DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 NVFP4 model is quantized with [Model Optimizer](https://github.com/NVIDIA/Model-Optimizer). This model is ready for commercial or non-commercial use.
## Third-Party Community Consideration This model is not owned or developed by NVIDIA. This model has been developed and built to a third-party's requirements for this application and use case; see link to Non-NVIDIA [(DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017) Model Card](https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017) from DeepSeek AI. ### License/Terms of Use: [MIT](https://huggingface.co/datasets/choosealicense/licenses/blob/main/markdown/mit.md) ### Deployment Geography: Global
### Use Case: Developers looking to take off-the-shelf, pre-quantized models for deployment in AI Agent systems, chatbots, RAG systems, and other AI-powered applications.
### Release Date: Hugging Face 10/30/2026 via https://huggingface.co/nvidia/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017-NVFP4
## References NVIDIA Model Optimizer: https://github.com/NVIDIA/Model-Optimizer ## Model Architecture: **Architecture Type:** Transformers
**Network Architecture:** DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 (`DeepseekV41ForCausalLM`) — Causal Encoder-Decoder Mixture-of-Experts with Compressed Sparse Attention 2
**Number of Model Parameters:** 552B backbone in total, 8B activated during prefill and 16B during decode, plus 196B Engram conditional memory
**This model was developed based on [DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017](https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017)**
## Input: **Input Type(s):** Text, Image
**Input Format(s):** String, Red, Green, Blue (RGB)
**Input Parameters:** One-Dimensional (1D), Two-Dimensional (2D)
**Other Properties Related to Input:** Context length up to 1M
## Output: **Output Type(s):** Text
**Output Format:** String
**Output Parameters:** One-Dimensional (1D): Sequences
**Other Properties Related to Output:** None
Our AI models are designed and/or optimized to run on NVIDIA GPU-accelerated systems. By leveraging NVIDIA's hardware (e.g. GPU cores) and software frameworks (e.g., CUDA libraries), the model achieves faster training and inference times compared to CPU-only solutions.
## Software Integration: **Supported Runtime Engine(s):**
* **vLLM** (needs MXFP4 Engram support, [vllm-project/vllm#61530](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/61530))
This checkpoint stores the Engram lookup tables as MXFP4, which stock vLLM images cannot load. Use a vLLM build that includes the pull request above. The benchmark results below were obtained with `vllm/vllm-openai:v0.31.0` with that pull request's Engram changes applied. SGLang has not been validated with this checkpoint. **Supported Hardware Microarchitecture Compatibility:**
* NVIDIA Blackwell
**Preferred Operating System(s):**
* Linux
The integration of foundation and fine-tuned models into AI systems requires additional testing using use-case-specific data to ensure safe and effective deployment. Following the V-model methodology, iterative testing and validation at both unit and system levels are essential to mitigate risks, meet technical and functional requirements, and ensure compliance with safety and ethical standards before deployment. ## Model Version(s): The model is quantized with nvidia-modelopt **v0.48.0rc0**. Source revision: `1bae0e1088993b9b82de08f59de5be5a34e42170`.
## Training and Evaluation Datasets: ## Calibration Dataset: **Link:** [cnn_dailymail](https://huggingface.co/datasets/abisee/cnn_dailymail), [Nemotron-Post-Training-Dataset-v2](https://huggingface.co/datasets/nvidia/Nemotron-Post-Training-Dataset-v2)
**Data Collection Method by dataset:** Automated.
**Labeling Method by dataset:** Automated.
**Properties:** The cnn_dailymail dataset is an English-language dataset containing just over 300k unique news articles as written by journalists at CNN and the Daily Mail. The Nemotron-Post-Training-Dataset-v2 is a post-training dataset curated by NVIDIA containing multi-turn conversations across diverse topics.
Calibration used 512 samples per dataset (1,024 total), sequence length 512, batch size 4, and the default deterministic sample selection. The Nemotron subsets were `stem`, `chat`, `math`, and `code`. ## Training Dataset: **Data Modality:** Undisclosed
**Data Collection Method by dataset:** Undisclosed
**Labeling Method by dataset:** Undisclosed
**Properties:** Undisclosed
## Evaluation Dataset: **Datasets:** GPQA Diamond, AA-LCR, SciCode, IFBench, MMMU-Pro, Terminal-Bench 2.1
**Data Collection Method by dataset:** Hybrid: Automated, Manually-Collected
**Labeling Method by dataset:** Hybrid: Manually-Labeled, Automated
**Properties:** These benchmarks cover scientific reasoning (GPQA Diamond), long-context recall (AA-LCR), scientific coding (SciCode), instruction following (IFBench), visual understanding (MMMU-Pro), and terminal-based agent tasks (Terminal-Bench 2.1).
## Inference: **Acceleration Engines:** **vLLM**
**Test Hardware:** **NVIDIA GB300 (Blackwell)**
## Post Training Quantization This model converts the ordinary routed MoE experts from source MXFP4 to NVFP4 weights and activations (W4A4), with group size 16. The converted projections are `w1`, `w2`, and `w3` for 384 experts across 40 layers. The Engram lookup tables are converted from the source FP8 to MXFP4. Attention, shared experts, vision, MTP, and other excluded components retain their source precision, including MXFP8 where applicable. All 16,986,931,200 expert weight blocks passed lossless conversion, preserving dequantized weight values with signed-zero canonicalization; the Engram conversion is lossy. Activation scales were calibrated; 24 of 46,080 projection entries used fallback scales. Lossless weight conversion does not imply identical inference outputs. The checkpoint is approximately 400 GiB (source: approximately 475 GiB) in 48 safetensors shards. ## Usage ### Deploy with vLLM This checkpoint needs a vLLM build with MXFP4 Engram support ([vllm-project/vllm#61530](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/61530)). The command below is the one used for the reported results on four GB300 GPUs, with the repository ID in place of the local path. ```bash VLLM_ENGINE_READY_TIMEOUT_S=3600 vllm serve nvidia/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017-NVFP4 \ --tensor-parallel-size 4 \ --tokenizer-mode deepseek_v41 \ --attention-config '{"backend":"FLASHINFER_MLA_SPARSE_DSV41","indexer_kv_dtype":"mxfp4","indexer_sparse_logits":true}' \ --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \ --max-num-seqs 128 \ --engram-config '{"cpu_offload":true}' \ --reasoning-parser deepseek_v41 ``` Add `--enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser deepseek_v41` for tool calling. Pass `chat_template_kwargs: {"thinking": true, "reasoning_effort": "max"}` in requests for thinking at maximum effort. Text and image input were validated with this command; speculative decoding (MTP) was not exercised. Validate the final staged package with the intended runtime before deployment. ## Evaluation Accuracy results obtained with vLLM are shown below, in percent.
Precision GPQA Diamond AA-LCR SciCode IFBench MMMU-Pro Terminal-Bench 2.1
MXFP4 (source) 92.77 80.41 57.58 76.33 78.38 81.81
NVFP4 + MXFP4 Engram 92.93 80.19 57.32 76.47 78.73 81.11
> Baseline: [DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017](https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017), a mixed-precision checkpoint with MXFP4 routed experts. > Ordinary benchmark requests used `temperature=1.0`, `top_p=1.0`, `reasoning_effort=max`, and `max_new_tokens=262144`. > GPQA used 16 repeats; AA-LCR used 16 repeats in each of two runs; IFBench used 5; SciCode is the mean of 8 runs. > Terminal-Bench 2.1 used a separate agentic configuration with eight trajectories per task; the score is the mean of two runs. ## Model Limitations: The base model was trained on data that contains toxic language and societal biases originally crawled from the internet. Therefore, the model may amplify those biases and return toxic responses especially when prompted with toxic prompts. The model may generate answers that may be inaccurate, omit key information, or include irrelevant or redundant text producing socially unacceptable or undesirable text, even if the prompt itself does not include anything explicitly offensive. ## Ethical Considerations NVIDIA believes Trustworthy AI is a shared responsibility and we have established policies and practices to enable development for a wide array of AI applications. Developers should work with their internal model team to ensure this model meets requirements for the relevant industry and use case and addresses unforeseen product misuse. Please make sure you have proper rights and permissions for all input image and video content; if image or video includes people, personal health information, or intellectual property, the image or video generated will not blur or maintain proportion

items.title: Managing Amazon Bedrock costs end to end: A playbook for FinOps and platform teams
items.summary: This post presents a five-stage operating model for managing Amazon Bedrock cost: attribute every dollar to an owner, make every request observable, enforce budgets, optimize platform defaults, and operate a review cadence. Written for FinOps and platform engineering teams.
items.content:
Artificial Intelligence 

 Managing Amazon Bedrock costs end to end: A playbook for FinOps and platform teams

 Cost management for generative AI is a shared responsibility between the teams that build applications and the teams accountable for cloud spend. Many teams start by comparing per-model token rates and asking application teams to shorten prompts. Those steps help, but they don’t answer the questions that finance and engineering leaders ask as usage scales: which team spent this, on which workload, and was that spend inside an approved budget?

 Agentic workloads make those questions more pressing. A conversational assistant typically issues one model invocation per user turn. An agentic workflow, such as an AI coding assistant that plans a change, reads files, calls tools, and iterates, issues many invocations per task and carries a larger context on each one. Token consumption therefore scales with the degree of autonomy you grant the workflow and the size of the context it carries, rather than with the number of user interactions. Because consumption is a function of how a workload is designed and operated, cost management for generative AI is an architectural and operational discipline. Published averages are a poor substitute for your own numbers: use the AWS Pricing Calculator and the Amazon Bedrock pricing page to model rates, and use Step 2 of this post to measure what your workloads actually consume.

 The fix isn’t a cheaper model or a smaller prompt. It’s an operating model: a repeatable loop that attributes every dollar to an owner, makes every request observable, alerts on and enforces budgets before overspend compounds, optimizes the platform defaults that drive most waste, and reviews the whole system on a cadence.

 In this post, you learn how to manage Amazon Bedrock cost in five steps. You attribute every dollar to an owner, make every request observable, control spend with budgets and enforcement, optimize the platform defaults that drive most avoidable spend, and operate a review cadence that turns data into decisions. This approach is built from AWS building blocks, and you can customize it and apply it to your own environment. The post is written for two audiences: FinOps practitioners who own attribution, chargeback, budgets, and anomaly review, and platform engineering teams who own logging, request metadata, enforcement, and routing defaults.

 The operating model in one view

 Five stages, run as a loop. Attribute: every Amazon Bedrock dollar lands on an identity, team, and application in the billing pipeline. Observe: every request is logged with enough metadata to explain what generated the spend. Enforce: budgets have teeth, with alerts at minimum and hard blocks where the risk demands them. Optimize: the platform defaults (model routing, caching, token limits) remove waste centrally instead of asking every team to be careful. Operate: a small scorecard and a review cadence turn the data into decisions. FinOps leads stages one and five. Platform engineering leads two through four. The review is joint. The stages are sequenced deliberately. Each one depends on the ones before it, and teams that jump straight to optimization without attribution and observability are guessing.

 Figure 1: The five-stage operating model, run as a continuous loop

 Stage 1: Attribute every dollar

 You can’t manage what you can’t attribute, and everything downstream (chargeback, budgets, enforcement, anomaly detection) depends on this stage. The foundation is the granular cost attribution of Amazon Bedrock (see Introducing granular cost attribution for Amazon Bedrock ): Amazon Bedrock automatically attributes inference costs to the AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) principal that made the call, across all models, with no resources to manage. The caller’s ARN lands in the line_item_iam_principal column of the AWS Cost and Usage Report (CUR) 2.0 , and coverage spans IAM users, roles, federated identities, and API keys.

 Setup is four steps:

 Turn on IAM principal data in your CUR 2.0 data export.

 Tag your IAM principals with business dimensions such as team, application, and cost center. For federated access, configure your identity provider to pass session names and tags through OIDC or SAML claims.

 Activate those tags as cost allocation tags in AWS Billing (console or the UpdateCostAllocationTagsStatus API).

 Analyze the tags: they surface in CUR 2.0 with an iamPrincipal/ prefix (for example, iamPrincipal/team ) and appear in AWS Cost Explorer under the IAM category within 24–48 hours of activation, ready for filtering and grouping by team, application, or cost center.

 This is invoice-grade, per-identity attribution with no custom infrastructure.

 The shared-role problem

 The pattern that deserves the most attention is the shared-role problem, because it is where most platforms silently lose attribution. A large language model (LLM) gateway that calls Amazon Bedrock through a single IAM role attributes every dollar to that one role, eliminating per-user visibility entirely. The fix is per-user session management. The gateway assumes the Amazon Bedrock invocation role once per user, passing the user’s identity as the role session name and their attributes as session tags, then caches those credentials for up to an hour (one AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) call per user per hour, not per request).

 This needs two roles: a gateway execution role holding sts:AssumeRole and sts:TagSession permissions, and the Amazon Bedrock invocation role it assumes. The result is line_item_iam_principal entries like assumed-role/BedrockRuntimeRole/gw-alex , each carrying its user’s tags: per-user and per-tenant attribution restored behind a shared gateway.

 import boto3

sts = boto3.client("sts")

# One call per user; cache the returned credentials up to 1 hour
response = sts.assume_role(
 RoleArn="arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/BedrockRuntimeRole",
 RoleSessionName="gw-alex", # the user, not the gateway
 Tags=[
 {"Key": "team", "Value": "sales-ai"},
 {"Key": "application", "Value": "renewal-agent"},
 {"Key": "costCenter", "Value": "CC-2041"}
 ]
) 

 A note on application inference profiles and Projects

 Amazon Bedrock offers two more attribution mechanisms, each suited to a different pattern. Application inference profiles are pre-created, per-application resources on the bedrock-runtime endpoint that carry cost allocation tags. You create one profile per application per model per AWS Region, and callers reference the profile ARN, which fits teams with a small and stable set of applications and models. Projects and workspaces serve the bedrock-mantle endpoint (Responses API, Chat Completions API). A project isn’t tied to a specific model, so a single project ID spans many models, which fits teams whose model usage changes frequently. You pass the project ID at client initialization, and its tags flow to CUR 2.0 and Cost Explorer (see Manage AI costs with Amazon Bedrock Projects ). Projects are the attribution path for OpenAI-compatible workloads on Amazon Bedrock.

 For bedrock-runtime workloads, we recommend IAM principal attribution through session tags as the primary mechanism. It scales with your identity system, requires no pre-created resources, and covers every model and API operation. Application inference profiles work well when a small, stable set of business units needs invoice-grade billing separation without changes to identity design. Use projects for bedrock-mantle workloads that use the Responses API or Chat Completions API.

 Stage 2: Make every request observable

 CUR tells you who spent. Invocation logs tell you what happened. Amazon Bedrock supports model invocation logging of request data, response data, and metadata to Amazon CloudWatch Logs, Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), or both. Use Amazon CloudWatch for fast operational queries and S3 plus Amazon Athena for long-term business intelligence (BI) access. Treat logging as infrastructure, not a manual toggle: provision the log group or bucket through code, define retention and encryption policies, and validate delivery during environment setup. If logging exists only in development or only in one Region, your cost program becomes fragmentary the moment usage grows.

 Logging also closes the latency gap: CUR attribution lags roughly 24 hours, but CloudWatch plus OpenTelemetry can power near-real-time dashboards showing per-developer spend within minutes ( Analyzing Claude Code usage with CloudWatch and OpenTelemetry demonstrates this end to end).

 Request metadata for workload-level attribution

 Raw logs answer identity-level questions. To answer workload-level questions (which feature, workflow, or tenant generated the tokens), stamp request metadata on every call. Amazon Bedrock captures this metadata in the invocation logs for later analysis:

 The following example uses Anthropic Claude Sonnet 5.5 on Amazon Bedrock through the US cross-Region inference profile. For the full list of models, see Supported foundation models in Amazon Bedrock . For availability by Region, see Model support by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock .

 response = client.converse(
 modelId="us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5-5",
 messages=[...],
 requestMetadata={
 "application": "renewal-copilot",
 "workflow": "renewal-risk-summary",
 "tenant": "enterprise-sales",
 "agent": "renewal-agent"
 }
) 

 Amazon Bedrock doesn’t enforce request metadata, and teams drift into inconsistent schemas quickly when every application does its own thing. The platform team should inject mandatory metadata centrally in a shared SDK wrapper or gateway, normalize the key set, and treat metadata coverage as a platform health metric.

 Diagnostic queries

 With logs and metadata in place, CloudWatch Logs Insights answers the standing questions. Who consumes the most tokens :

 fields @timestamp, identity.arn as caller, modelId,
input.inputTokenCount as inToke

items.title: Preview web apps live as your coding agent builds them with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime
items.summary: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Session endpoints give each runtime session an authenticated URL that forwards any HTTP method, path, and WebSocket connection to the ports you allow. In this post, you deploy a coding agent that keeps a Vite website running in its session, then watch the live site update in your browser as the agent edits files.
items.content:
Artificial Intelligence 

 Preview web apps live as your coding agent builds them with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime

 Coding agents now build working web apps: a dashboard, a product page, a prototype that a product team wants to try. The fastest way to review that work is to open the app, use it, ask for a change, and check the result. That loop works well when the app keeps running where the agent edits it, so each change shows up in the browser within seconds. When the app must be copied out and deployed somewhere else first, every change waits for a deployment, and the review slows down to that pace.

 Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with your choice of agent framework and foundation model (FM). AgentCore runtime , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, runs each agent session in its own isolated microVM. With Session endpoints , you can open an app running in that session from your own browser. Session Endpoints give each session an authenticated URL that forwards each request’s HTTP method, path, query string, and body, and WebSocket connections, to the ports you allow. You can watch the page update as the agent saves each file.

 In this post, you deploy a coding agent that keeps a Vite website running in its session, then open one local page with a chat on the left and the live website on the right. You ask the agent to switch the site to a dark color theme, follow its steps as they stream in, and watch the website change without a refresh. Finally, you look at what happens internally: a second port in the same session, and the requests the Session endpoint refuses.

 The complete sample, including the notebook this post follows, is in the 14-remote-access folder of the agentcore-samples GitHub repo .

 How Session endpoints work

 Each session gets its own Session endpoint, and six details shape how you use it.

 You choose which ports it reaches.  You set allowedPorts when you call CreateAgentRuntime : 1–5 entries, each a single port or a range within 8000–12000, excluding the reserved platform ports . Allowing a port doesn’t start a server, so your application must listen on it, bound to 0.0.0.0 .

 The URL arrives with the session. The InvokeAgentRuntime response carries it in the X-Amzn-Bedrock-AgentCore-Runtime-Session-Endpoint-Url header, which SDKs that model it expose as sessionEndpointUrl .

 Every request is authenticated. For a runtime that uses AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) , each HTTP request, HTTP/2 stream, and WebSocket handshake carries a Signature Version 4 (SigV4) signature. The caller also needs bedrock-agentcore:InvokeAgentRuntimeProxy on the runtime and its runtime endpoint. For a runtime with an inbound JSON Web Token (JWT) authorizer , each request carries a bearer token instead. Knowing the URL doesn’t grant access.

 The host name selects the port. Your client connects on port 443 regardless of the target port, and a prefix on the host name chooses the port inside the session:

 https://8090--<session-endpoint-id>.runtime.bedrock-agentcore.<region>.on.aws/index.html
https://8081--<session-endpoint-id>.runtime.bedrock-agentcore.<region>.on.aws/status 

 It carries the protocols your server speaks. HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 requests, including server-sent events and gRPC, and WebSocket connections all pass through. This walkthrough uses HTTP/1.1 and WebSocket.

 It’s scoped to one session. The URL needs credentials on every request and lasts only as long as the session, so use it to build, test, and review what your agent produces. To serve an app to your users, deploy it to a hosting service such as AWS Amplify Hosting .

 A browser can’t add a SigV4 signature or a bearer token to the requests a page makes on its own, so the Session endpoint client in the bedrock-agentcore SDK can open a local endpoint on your machine. Your browser opens http://localhost:8088 , and the local endpoint adds your credentials to each request and WebSocket handshake before forwarding it.

 A Session endpoint is different from a runtime endpoint , which AgentCore runtime already provides. Use a runtime endpoint, such as DEFAULT , to reach your agent, which controls which version of it callers will reach. InvokeAgentRuntime calls resolve through it, so you can keep development and production on different versions and promote or roll back without changing callers. Use a Session endpoint to see what your agent runs in its session, such as a web preview. It’s an authenticated URL that reaches only the ports you allow, works with whichever version the session runs, and stops working when the session ends. For complete documentation, refer to Connect to runtime sessions through a session endpoint .

 Solution overview

 The sample has four parts. A coding agent runs in the session on port 8080 and edits the website’s files with four tools: list, read, write, and edit. The agent starts a Vite development server on port 8090, which serves the website and pushes each saved change to the browser over its hot-reload WebSocket. On your machine, PreviewApp serves the preview page, sends your prompts to InvokeAgentRuntime , and opens a local endpoint for the website. As Figure 1 shows, the preview page loads the website from the Vite development server on port 8090 through the local endpoint and the Session endpoint, and sends your prompts through InvokeAgentRuntime to the agent on port 8080. The numbers show the order of the steps for one request.

 Figure 1: Solution architecture

 Before step 1, PreviewApp has already called InvokeAgentRuntime once to start the session, which starts the agent and the Vite development server. PreviewApp read the Session endpoint URL from that response and opened a local endpoint for port 8090. The numbered steps in Figure 1 then follow one request for a change:

 The site pane of the preview page loads the website from the local endpoint on localhost:8088 . The local endpoint adds your credentials to each request and the WebSocket handshake, and forwards them to the Session endpoint. The Session endpoint checks the signature and the port against allowedPorts , then forwards them to the Vite development server on port 8090. The page keeps the Vite hot-reload WebSocket open.

 You send a prompt from the chat pane. PreviewApp sends it to InvokeAgentRuntime as a standard AWS API call signed with your AWS credentials, and the runtime delivers it to the agent on port 8080. The agent’s steps stream back to the chat pane as it works.

 The agent calls Claude Haiku 5.5 in Amazon Bedrock to decide what to change.

 The agent reads the site’s files and saves the ones it changes. The Vite development server serves those files and watches them for changes.

 When a file is saved, Vite pushes the change over the WebSocket opened in step 1, back through the Session endpoint and the local endpoint, and the site pane updates without a refresh.

 From the notebook, PreviewApp reads the agent’s /status route on port 8081 through the same Session endpoint. Only the port changes.

 Port 8080 isn’t in allowedPorts , because InvokeAgentRuntime reaches the agent without going through the Session endpoint.

 Prerequisites

 To follow the walkthrough, you need:

 An AWS account in an AWS Region where AgentCore runtime Session endpoints are available, with credentials configured.

 Permissions to create an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role, upload to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) , and create a runtime, plus bedrock-agentcore:InvokeAgentRuntime and bedrock-agentcore:InvokeAgentRuntimeProxy on that runtime and its DEFAULT runtime endpoint. For details, refer to IAM permissions for AgentCore runtime .

 Python 3.10 or later, with bedrock-agentcore 1.25.2 or later and boto3 1.43.122 or later.

 Git , to clone the sample repo, and a Jupyter environment, such as JupyterLab or Visual Studio Code with the Jupyter extension, to run the notebook.

 Access to Claude Haiku 5.5 in Amazon Bedrock. For model availability by Region, refer to Regional availability by models .

 Node.js 22 or later with npm , which the deployment script uses to package the agent and the website.

 The sample deploys the agent as a zip file in Amazon S3 with direct code deployment for Node.js , so you don’t need Docker or an Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) repository. Session endpoints work with microVM runtimes, not with the Instances compute type, and Session endpoint URLs are reachable over public HTTPS. AWS PrivateLink isn’t supported for inbound connections.

 Deploy the agent and its website

 First, you deploy the runtime, and the configuration you choose here decides which ports the Session endpoint can reach. The deployment script bundles the agent into one file, adds the website and its dependencies for the runtime’s Linux on Arm64 system, uploads the zip to Amazon S3, and creates the runtime.

 The following excerpt from deploy.py shows the two settings that matter for this post. protocolConfiguration says where the agent listens for InvokeAgentRuntime , and allowedPorts lists the ports the Session endpoint can reach: 8090 for the website and 8081 for the agent’s status route. Port 8080 isn’t in the list, because InvokeAgentRuntime reaches the agent without it. For the port and path settings, refer to Configure your agent’s serving port and invocation path .

 agentRuntimeArtifact={"codeConfiguration": {
 "code": {"s3": {"bucket": code_bucket(), "prefix": S3_PREFIX}},
 "runtime": "NODE_22",
 "entryPoint": ["app.js"],
}},
protocolConfiguration={"serverProtocol": "HTTP", "port": 8080, "path": "/invocations"},
allowedPorts=[{"port": 8090}, {"port": 8081}], 

 The website’s Vite configuration makes the development server reachable from the Session endpoint. It listens on 0.0.0.0 at port 8090 and doesn’t restrict the Host header ( server.allowedHosts is true), because requests arrive under a host name the runtime assigns rather

items.title: How Worldwide Express automated freight exceptions with Amazon Bedrock
items.summary: Worldwide Express automated its less-than-truckload freight billing-exception process with a multi-agent solution built on Amazon Bedrock. Six months after launch, the company cut active exceptions by 75%, improved time-to-cash by four weeks, and unlocked $10 million in free cash flow.
items.content:
Artificial Intelligence 

 How Worldwide Express automated freight exceptions with Amazon Bedrock

 Worldwide Express (part of ShipStation Global) had built something big: approximately $5 billion in systemwide revenue, over 75 less-than-truckload (LTL) carriers and more than 130,000 customers. But that same scale had a hidden cost. Every month, $15 million in free cash flow sat frozen, locked in billing exceptions no one had resolved yet. Each one had to be chased down by hand, carrier by carrier, with its own rules to check. Worldwide Express outsourced to a team that worked cases one at a time, calling customers and carriers for each dispute. The exceptions piled up, cash stayed stuck, and every order took longer to turn into money.

 Worldwide Express worked with AWS and LTM to build a multi-agentic AI solution with Amazon Bedrock that plugs directly into their transportation management system (TMS), SpeedShip. Six months after launch, the company reported a 75 percent reduction in active exceptions, a 4-week improvement in time-to-cash, $1M annual savings, and a one-time $10M free cash flow infusion.

 In this post, we describe the challenge, explain how Worldwide Express designed the multi-agent solution, and share the results.

 The challenge

 In LTL freight, roughly 14 percent of invoices fail the standard three-way match between the purchase order, the goods receipt, and the carrier invoice. When a match fails, the invoice enters exception handling. For Worldwide Express, exceptions fell into three categories:

 Line-item mismatches: Quantities or service codes that didn’t align with the shipment record.

 Pricing variances: The carrier billed a rate different from the contracted price.

 Unexpected accessorial charges: Liftgate fees, residential surcharges, or reweigh adjustments that weren’t on the original quote.

 Each exception triggered a five-step manual process:

 Identify the exception type by cross-referencing the invoice against the purchase order, goods receipt, and pricing.

 Research the root cause in vendor records.

 Send email to the carrier or warehouse with dispute details.

 Wait for a response.

 Execute the resolution in the TMS.

 With each carrier operating under its own tariff structure and dispute workflow, this process consumed most of the FinOps team’s bandwidth.

 Rule-based process automation (RPA) can handle structured, predictable workflows. However, exception resolution requires contextual judgment: interpreting a carrier’s accessorial policy, comparing charges against shipment data, and deciding validity given a carrier, exception type, and dollar amount. That variability is what made the problem a fit for the agentic AI framework.

 From assessment to production

 In June 2025, Worldwide Express engaged the AWS Business Transformation & Value Advisory team to identify 19 automation opportunities across the Order-to-Cash lifecycle. Knowing the business value of exceptions automation, Worldwide Express moved from assessment to production in less than 6 months.

 How it works

 The solution runs on AWS. Amazon Bedrock provides AI reasoning, and Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) is the engine. The design calls for fine-grained control over how each agent reasons, where decision boundaries sit, and how exceptions are routed between agents. Building the framework directly on Amazon EC2, with Amazon Bedrock providing inference, keeps that orchestration logic fully in the team’s hands and supports open source agent libraries. Production controls of business logic make each agent’s role, inputs, and decision boundaries explicit and auditable. In a billing-dispute workflow, every automated decision needs to be explainable.

 Agents

 When an invoice exception is detected, the system routes it to one of three specialized AI agents, each handling a specific type of billing dispute:

 Invoice Matching Agent finds the matching shipment record and flags what doesn’t line up.

 Pricing Variance Agent compares the carrier’s charge against the contracted rate and determines whether the difference is valid.

 Accessorial Validation Agent checks whether unexpected fees (such as residential delivery or liftgate charges) are supported by the actual delivery events.

 Each agent pulls specific carrier billing rules and policies before making a recommendation. After the exception is resolved, the system generates a plain-language note explaining what was found and what action was taken.

 Each custom agent has an instruction prompt (defining its role, decision boundaries, and output format), a set of actions (integrations into SpeedShip), and access to carrier-specific knowledge bases. By using Amazon Bedrock, each agent accesses a suitable foundation model through a single API while inheriting existing AWS governance. For model availability by Region, refer to Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock .

 Actions

 The agents connect to SpeedShip through the same APIs that analysts use. That means the AI sees exactly what a human reviewer would see (contract rates, shipment details, delivery proof) and writes its resolution into the same workflow. SpeedShip has APIs on AWS, so the agents wire into the same endpoints as other existing systems.

 Carrier knowledge base

 Every carrier has different billing rules, fee definitions, and dispute procedures. Worldwide Express stores each carrier’s documentation: tariff rules, surcharge definitions, dispute steps, and variance thresholds. When an agent processes an exception, it retrieves that specific carrier’s policies and standard operating procedure (SOP) documents before deciding, so each decision is grounded in the carrier’s own rules. The same three agents handle all carriers without any carrier-specific code.

 Human-in-the-loop

 The approval step was necessary for FinOps adoption during the initial rollout. Initially, a human reviewer would use the existing SpeedShip UI to approve recommendations before they’re finalized. Eventually when accuracy exceeded 99 percent, bulk approval became the default.

 Observability

 Worldwide Express’s team built dashboards tracking automation rate by carrier, error rate by exception type, resolution time, and human override frequency. When a reviewer rejects a recommendation, the system logs the feedback. The team refines instruction prompts and knowledge bases based on rejection history, steadily increasing automation coverage.

 End-to-end flow

 The following diagram shows the end-to-end flow, from exception detection through the three specialized agents to human approval. In the diagram, exceptions from the data sources (the SpeedShip TMS, a shipping system, an electronic data interchange (EDI) server, and carrier and vendor portals) are detected and routed to one of three agents. Each agent runs on Amazon EC2 with Auto Scaling, uses an agent framework with its own prompt, tools, and carrier knowledge base, and calls Amazon Bedrock for model inference. The agents produce a resolution report. Cost finalization and an AI-written note then go to a human reviewer for approval in the SpeedShip analyst UI.

 Figure 1: Worldwide Express’s AI-powered exception handling architecture on AWS

 Results

 Six months in, Worldwide Express has deployed the solution across over 40 LTL carriers. The agents currently close 10,000 (approximately 50 percent) exceptions weekly with a less than 1 percent error rate. This shifted the FinOps team’s time from routine resolution to complex, high-value disputes.

 The impact shows up most clearly in the backlog of active exceptions, which fell from $15M in June 2025 to $4M six months later, a 75 percent reduction. Worldwide Express unlocked $10M in freed-up cash flow, over $1M in annual cost savings, and 60x first-year ROI. The company reports time-to-cash improving by four weeks.

 “With AWS, we’ve automated more than 40 percent of weekly billing exceptions, significantly reducing costs and accelerating billing cycles from days to minutes. Today, we release approximately $10 million more in customer billings each week at a speed that simply wasn’t possible before.” 

 — Nathanael Pearson, VP of FinOps, Worldwide Express

 Looking forward

 Worldwide Express is already expanding this approach to other parts of the Order-to-Cash cycle. For logistics companies managing high carrier volumes, the path forward is to start small. Automate the most repetitive exception type first, prove accuracy, then scale across the rest of the portfolio.

 Conclusion

 Worldwide Express’s exception automation shows what’s possible when agentic AI meets a well-scoped business problem. The combination of Amazon Bedrock, carrier-specific knowledge bases, and a human-in-the-loop approval design let Worldwide Express move from assessment to production in less than 6 months while maintaining financial controls. The company is now expanding automation to other Order-to-Cash processes.

 To explore whether a similar approach might work for your organization, request a conversation with your account team or learn more about Amazon Bedrock . Partners like LTM can run a Proof of Value sprint with your own data.

 Build a Validated Kubernetes Runtime for NVIDIA Dynamo

 Oct 30, 2026

 By Stefan Schimanski , Jamie Li and Yuan Chen 

 Like

 Discuss (0)

 L 

 T 

 F 

 R 

 E 

 AI-Generated Summary

 NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform packages NVIDIA Dynamo and its supporting infrastructure into validated recipes through NVIDIA AI Cluster Runtime (AICR).
 AICR captures runtime requirements such as GPU driver stacks, Dynamic Resource Allocation, gang scheduling, node health signals, and Prometheus metrics in reproducible recipes with pinned component versions.
 Dynamo 1.4.2 uses TCP for the request plane and ZMQ for KV-cache events, enabling both the native Dynamo Frontend router and the Gateway API Inference Extension (GAIE) / Endpoint Picker Plugin (EPP) path to make cache-aware routing decisions.
 The Dynamo Frontend router path suits model-specific endpoints with the smallest serving topology, while the GAIE/EPP path integrates with shared Kubernetes ingress managed through Gateway API resources.
 AICR separates runtime setup from application deployment through a five-step flow: snapshot the cluster, generate a Dynamo inference recipe, render a deployment bundle, deploy the runtime with Helmfile or GitOps, and validate the installed runtime before installing application workloads.
 Next Steps
 Explore the NVIDIA AI Cluster Runtime (AICR) to configure and validate inference infrastructure.
 Explore the NVIDIA Dynamo repository for the distributed inference framework.
 Join the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Slack community for discussion and hands-on workshops.

 Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information.  Learn more 

 Teams building AI applications need a repeatable path from a model configuration to a working inference endpoint. NVIDIA Dynamo is a distributed inference framework that coordinates model serving across GPU workers. Deploying it on Kubernetes is only a first step. A successful model deployment requires more: GPU drivers, resource allocation, scheduling, networking, and monitoring must all work together. Resolving these dependencies takes time away from testing model behavior, serving performance, and application integration.

 The NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform brings together technologies to help the ecosystem design, build, and operate more efficient AI factories, and Dynamo is one of them. To make management of those infrastructure dependencies easier, the platform contains NVIDIA AI Cluster Runtime (AICR). It packages NVIDIA Dynamo and its supporting infrastructure into validated recipes. Each recipe defines a configuration for a specific environment and workload, including pinned component versions, compatibility constraints, and validation checks. AICR gives platform teams a repeatable way to deploy and check the runtime, providing developers with a consistent foundation for serving models and testing applications.

 This walkthrough covers the infrastructure that supports Dynamo on Kubernetes, compares two routing options, and shows how to deploy and validate the runtime with AICR.

 Why the underlying runtime matters for Dynamo 

 Running a model with Dynamo on Kubernetes starts with a DynamoGraphDeployment that specifies how vLLM , SGLang , or NVIDIA TensorRT LLM should run in pods on the cluster. But the graph is only the top of the stack. A production inference cluster also needs a runtime layer below it. It has to answer questions like:

 Is the NVIDIA GPU Operator installed with a driver stack that matches the nodes?

 Are GPU nodes labeled and discoverable?

 Does the cluster expose GPUs through the expected Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) driver?

 Can the scheduler place GPU workers with the required topology and gang scheduling semantics?

 Are node health signals available before workloads land on a degraded node?

 Is Prometheus reachable for Dynamo and accelerator metrics?

 Is the Gateway API / Endpoint Picker (EPP) path configured when the deployment should be Kubernetes-native at ingress?

 AICR captures these runtime requirements in the recipe.

 What AICR ships for Dynamo 

 An AICR Dynamo recipe packages both Dynamo and the cluster runtime components it depends on.

 AICR ships version 1.4.2 of the dynamo-platform chart, which includes the Dynamo operator, Dynamo runtime images, and resources such as the nvidia.com/v1beta1 DynamoGraphDeployment CustomResourceDefinition (CRD) . v1beta1 replaces the former v1alpha1 API version.

 Table 1 lists the supporting infrastructure components included in the recipe.

 Prerequisite Requirement Component in the AICR recipe 
 GPU driver stack Driver and GPU software stack that matches the nodes NVIDIA GPU Operator 
 GPU discovery GPU nodes labeled and discoverable for placement Node Feature Discovery 
 GPU allocation GPUs exposed through Kubernetes-native Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) DRA Driver for NVIDIA GPUs 
 Scheduling GPU workers placed with the required topology and gang scheduling KAI Scheduler 
 Inference Workload Orchestration Multi-component serving graphs started, placed, and scaled as coordinated groups Grove 
 Node health Health signals available before workloads land on a degraded node NVSentinel and Nodewright , where supported by the selected recipe 
 Metrics Cluster, accelerator, and Dynamo service metrics collected Prometheus stack 
 Ingress Gateway / EPP path configured when ingress is Kubernetes-native agentgateway and Gateway API resources, described in the routing sections 
 Table 1. Runtime prerequisites below Dynamo and the components the AICR recipe installs for each 

 In addition, the recipe pins component versions and records configuration values, node selectors, tolerations, checksums, and validation expectations to make deployment reproducible.

 With Dynamo 1.4, frontends, workers, optional Gateway API Inference Extension (GAIE) / Endpoint Picker Plugin (EPP) components , and other Dynamo services discover each other through Kubernetes resources. AICR’s default path therefore no longer uses NATS, and the dynamo-platform chart no longer installs it by default. NATS remains available as an opt-in for deployments that need it.

 Agentic workloads repeatedly extend long token prefixes, including system prompts, tool definitions, conversation history, and tool results. If a turn reaches a worker without that prefix in GPU memory, the system reprocesses intermediate tokens instead of reusing cached results. Dynamo routes requests to workers that already hold the relevant KV blocks, either through its frontend router or through GAIE/EPP integration at the Gateway API layer.

 Dynamo can also separate prompt processing (prefill) from token generation (decode), an architecture known as disaggregated serving. On KV-cache misses, all or part of the prompt must be reprocessed by the prefill pool. Decode workers then take over token-by-token generation, which has different GPU, memory, latency, and batching characteristics. The cache miss rate depends on the workload. Long-running agentic sessions behave differently from one-off chat requests. Disaggregated serving enables operators to scale and tune prefill and decode capacity independently for a given request mix.

 The request plane and KV-cache event plane are separate. In Dynamo 1.4.2, the default AICR Kubernetes path uses TCP for requests and ZMQ for KV-cache events. Each vLLM worker engine emits raw KV-cache events through a local ZMQ publisher, for example, with the following vLLM configuration:

--enable-prefix-caching --kv-transfer-config \
 {"enable_kv_cache_events": true, "publisher": "zmq", "endpoint": "tcp://*:5557"}

 Dynamo’s worker runtime then subscribes to that local vLLM event source, normalizes the events, and republishes them onto the Dynamo event plane. Both the native Dynamo Frontend router and the GAIE/EPP path use this Dynamo-managed KV-cache state to make routing decisions.

 What are the Dynamo routing paths on Kubernetes? 

 Dynamo supports two routing paths on Kubernetes. The first uses the Dynamo Frontend router for worker selection. The second uses a Kubernetes Gateway API implementation for ingress and Dynamo EPP for endpoint selection. AICR ships and validates the Dynamo runtime for either topology.

 Path 1: Dynamo Frontend router 

 The default path exposes a Dynamo Frontend behind a Kubernetes Service. Running with DYN_ROUTER_MODE=kv , the Frontend tokenizes each request, scores eligible workers using prefix overlap and current load, selects a worker, and dispatches the request through the Dynamo request plane, which uses TCP by default.

 This path is suitable when an application team owns a model-specific endpoint or an existing edge proxy only needs to forward traffic to the Dynamo Frontend Service. It is the smallest topology for deploying and validating a Dynamo graph and is the most production-proven serving option. It does not require the additional gateway and EPP components used in Path 2.

 Figure 1. The Dynamo Frontend selects a vLLM worker based on KV-cache overlap and load. Requests use the TCP request plane; worker KV-cache events reach the Frontend through the ZMQ-backed event plane 

 Path 2: Gateway API Inference Extension and Dynamo EPP 

 This path integrates Dynamo with the Gateway API and Gateway API Inference Extension (GAIE). In the AICR example, agentgateway resolves an HTTPRoute to an InferencePool . The Dynamo operator creates that InferencePool from the DynamoGraphDeployment : its selector identifies eligible worker pods, while its endpointPickerRef identifies the Dynamo EPP Service.

 The gateway invokes the Dynamo EPP through GAIE’s endpoint-selection interface. The EPP tokenizes the request and uses Dynamo’s KV router to select an endpoint. It returns the selection and routing metadata to the gateway implementation, which is the actual HTTP proxy. In this mode, each routable worker pod includes a Dynamo Frontend si

Developer Tools & Techniques 

 Run AI Models for Edge Application Development with Just a Few Commands

 NVIDIA TensorRT Edge-LLM makes it easy to get started with AI development for embedded devices on the NVIDIA DGX Spark 64GB.

 Oct 30, 2026

 By Joe Halabi , Lin Chai , Maximilien Breughe , Michael Ferry and Charlotte Mallo 

 Like

 Discuss (0)

 L 

 T 

 F 

 R 

 E 

 AI-Generated Summary

 NVIDIA DGX Spark 64GB provides a platform for embedded developers to prototype, fine-tune, and test AI models and agents.
 TensorRT Edge-LLM delivers a lightweight C++ inference runtime that spans development on DGX Spark and deployment on Jetson Thor, DRIVE AGX Thor, and IGX Thor.
 The trtedge CLI downloads models and builds optimized TensorRT engines, enabling a chat session with Nemotron-3.5 Lightning in a few commands.
 An OpenAI-compatible API server can serve the model locally for application prototyping and testing.
 DSpark speculative decoding with three draft tokens increases mean generation speed from 73.4 to 126.9 tokens per second on HumanEval prompts while peak memory use remains 27.9GB.
 Next Steps
 Try another model from the supported models list to continue developing your application on Spark.
 Explore the TensorRT Edge-LLM documentation for model-specific workflows and requirements on your target embedded platform.
 Visit the Nemotron developer page for resources to get started with Nemotron models and datasets.

 Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information.  Learn more 

 AI is expanding beyond the data center as developers build a new generation of agents to act at the edge: monitoring driver attention and cabin conditions, helping robots understand their surroundings and plan tasks, and coordinating fleets of machines on production lines. These physical AI applications rely on models that perceive, reason, and act within tight memory, power, and latency budgets. But getting a model ready to run can involve substantial setup.

 NVIDIA DGX Spark, now available in a 64GB configuration , gives embedded developers a platform to prototype, fine-tune, and test models and agents. NVIDIA TensorRT Edge-LLM provides a lightweight C++ inference runtime designed for embedded workloads, bringing the same inference framework to development on Spark and deployment on platforms such as NVIDIA Jetson Thor , NVIDIA DRIVE AGX Thor , and NVIDIA IGX Thor .

 You can get started in just a few commands with the trtedge command-line interface (CLI). It downloads your selected model and builds TensorRT engines optimized for inference on Spark.

 In this tutorial, you’ll run NVIDIA Nemotron-3.5 Lightning , a text-only model, on Spark using TensorRT Edge-LLM. You’ll test prompts in your terminal and serve the model through an API for application prototyping. You’ll also enable DSpark speculative decoding to accelerate generation.

 Prerequisites: Set up your development environment 

 To get started, you’ll need a DGX Spark with a supported NVIDIA software stack, NVIDIA CUDA 13, TensorRT 10.16.1.11 or newer within the 10.x series, and Python 3.10 to 3.12. The examples below were tested with TensorRT Edge-LLM 0.11.1 and TensorRT 10.16.1.11.

 Open a terminal on your DGX Spark, create and activate a virtual environment, and install TensorRT Edge-LLM:

python3 -m venv --system-site-packages .venv-edgellm
source .venv-edgellm/bin/activate
python -m pip install --upgrade pip
python -m pip install "tensorrt-edgellm[server]==0.11.1"

 Note: The virtual environment keeps newly installed packages separate while allowing access to all system Python packages, including TensorRT.

 Check the TensorRT version and confirm that the TensorRT Edge-LLM runtime loads:

python -c "import tensorrt as trt; v = tuple(map(int, trt.__version__.split('.'))); assert (10, 16, 1, 11) <= v < (11,), f'TensorRT >=10.16.1.11 and <11 required; found {trt.__version__}'; from tensorrt_edgellm import runtime; runtime.load()"

 Note: If compatible system TensorRT bindings are unavailable, follow the NVIDIA TensorRT pip installation instructions to install a compatible TensorRT 10.x version in the activated environment, then rerun the verification command.

 With the virtual environment still active, start a chat with Nemotron-3.5 Lightning:

trtedge chat nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-NVFP4

 On your first launch, wait for the model download (approximately 21GB) and engine build to finish. Files are stored in ~/.cache/tensorrt-edgellm by default, so allow space for both the model and engines. Later launches reuse matching cached engines.

 Once the chat prompt appears, enter:

Convert 25°C to Fahrenheit. Answer in one sentence.

 Example response:

25°C is equal to 77°F.

 Continue the conversation with follow-up questions, or type /exit to end the session.

 Serve your model 

 Serve your model through a local OpenAI-compatible API on Spark for application development and testing.

 With your virtual environment active, start the server:

trtedge serve nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-NVFP4 \
 --host 127.0.0.1 \
 --port 8000

 The server builds or reuses an engine for this configuration. Once startup completes, open a second terminal on your DGX Spark and check that it is ready:

curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8000/health/ready 

 A response containing "status":"ready" confirms that the server is ready. Send your first prompt to the chat completions endpoint:

curl -fsS -N http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/chat/completions \
 -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
 -d '{
 "model": "nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-NVFP4",
 "messages": [
 {
 "role": "user",
 "content": "Convert 25°C to Fahrenheit. Answer in one sentence."
 }
 ],
 "stream": true,
 "temperature": 0,
 "max_tokens": 128
}'

 The response streams as JSON events. Keep the server running for more requests, or press Ctrl+C in the server terminal to stop it.

 Optional: Enable speculative decoding 

 You can speed up generation with DSpark speculative decoding , which uses a draft model to propose several tokens for the main model to verify in a single pass. To enable it with three draft tokens, press Ctrl+C in the server terminal, then restart the server with DSpark enabled:

trtedge serve nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-NVFP4 \
 --host 127.0.0.1 \
 --port 8000 \
 --speculative-config '{
 "method": "dspark", 
 "model": "nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-NVFP4-DSpark",
 "num_speculative_tokens": 3
 }'

 Once the server is ready, send another prompt to the chat completions endpoint to try DSpark-enabled generation.

 You can experiment with num_speculative_tokens and other settings to tune generation speed for your workload. See the speculative decoding documentation to learn more .

 Performance on DGX Spark 64GB 

 TensorRT Edge-LLM delivers low response latency and fast token generation with NVIDIA Nemotron-3.5 Lightning on DGX Spark 64GB.

 The table below reports time to first token (TTFT) and generation speed with and without DSpark speculative decoding.

 Decoding Workload Median TTFT (ms) Mean generation speed (tokens/s) 
 DSpark OFF SpeedBench 1K 201.0 73.3 
 DSpark OFF SpeedBench 2K 329.5 72.8 
 DSpark OFF HumanEval prompts 98.1 73.4 

 DSpark ON SpeedBench 1K 203.0 108.5 
 DSpark ON SpeedBench 2K 331.6 105.3 
 DSpark ON HumanEval prompts 98.7 126.9 
 Table 1. Nemotron-3.5 Lightning performance on DGX Spark 64GB with and without DSpark speculative decoding. 

 Generation speed is the average token generation rate per request, excluding time to first token. DSpark uses three draft tokens. Peak total system memory use during inference with DSpark was 27.9GB, including the OS.

 Measured on DGX Spark 64GB running DGX OS 7.6.0 (Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS), using NVFP4 with thinking enabled, batch size one, one concurrent streaming request, and a 128-token output limit. Average input lengths were 1,153 tokens for SpeedBench 1K, 2,247 for SpeedBench 2K, and 139 for HumanEval.

 Next steps 

 Try another model from the supported models list and continue developing your application on Spark. Options include vision-language models that interpret images and video, as well as speech recognition and text-to-speech models.

 Explore the TensorRT Edge-LLM documentation for model-specific workflows and requirements on your target embedded platform.

 And visit the Nemotron developer page for resources to get started. Explore open Nemotron models and datasets on Hugging Face and Blueprints on build.nvidia.com .

 About Joe Halabi

 Joe Halabi is a senior deep learning software engineer at NVIDIA, working on TensorRT Edge-LLM to optimize large language model inference for edge platforms. His work spans GPU kernel development, runtime systems, and power and performance optimization. Previously, he worked on the NVIDIA cuDNN library, developing just-in-time compilation capabilities and optimizing GPU kernels for LLM workloads. He holds a master’s degree in computer science from the University of California, Los Angeles.

Drawing on her background in autonomous driving and automotive OEMs, she is inspired to build production-grade inference systems that deliver best-in-class performance for deep learning workloads across data center, edge, and physical AI applications—enabling systems that perceive, reason, and act in the real world.
